title: Title and date
short: Written in 1857 and titled 'Nonsense' in manuscript, the poem appeared as 'Winter: My Secret' in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862).
body: The archive prints the poem as 'My Secret'. In Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) it was called 'Winter: My Secret'. Rossetti's manuscript, from 1857, called it 'Nonsense', which marks the piece as light verse and teasing. The opening line starts in the middle of a conversation, as if answering a request to confess, and the poem spends its whole length refusing. Critics have offered very different accounts of the 'secret'. Biographical readings look for a hidden love. Others take the poem as a play on the reticence of a woman poet, or on the reader's wish to read her lyrics as confessions.

title: fie
short: An old exclamation of reproach or mock disgust, used here with playful coyness.
body: 'Fie' is an interjection that expresses reproach or (often playfully) disgust. By the nineteenth century it sounded old-fashioned or nursery-like. Its use sets the tone. The speaker scolds the questioner for being 'too curious', but lightly, flirting rather than taking offence. The short broken lines of the first stanza ('You want to hear it? well:') imitate a spoken exchange and make the reader the one who is being teased.

title: Irregular form
short: Line lengths and rhymes vary freely, and the poem moves through winter, spring and summer in four verse paragraphs.
body: The poem has no fixed stanza. Lines run from two stresses to five, and rhymes come back unpredictably (shows / nose / snows / blows in the long second verse paragraph; me / me). In st. 2 there are bursts of internal and chiming rhyme, 'bounding and surrounding', 'buffeting, astounding', 'Nipping and clipping'. This freedom suits the tone of conversation and keeps the reader guessing, as the speaker does. Its structure follows the seasons. Winter (the long st. 2) justifies concealment, spring (st. 3) cannot be trusted, and summer (st. 4) is a conditional 'perhaps'. The title 'Winter: My Secret' links the secret to the cold season.

title: Perhaps there's none
short: The speaker suggests the secret may not exist, 'only just my fun', which makes the poem a game about withholding.
body: Suddenly the speaker suggests there may be nothing to tell, so the secret becomes a pose. This turn is central to the main critical readings. If the secret is empty, the poem is about the reader's appetite for the poet's private life and about the power of keeping something back. If it is real, the denial is one more layer of disguise. Rossetti leaves both open. Biographical theories exist (critics have linked the poem to her relations with men), but they rest on thin evidence.

title: nipping day
short: 'Nipping' (sharply cold, biting) may recall Hamlet's 'nipping and an eager air' on the battlements.
body: To nip is to pinch or bite, and of cold it means sharp, frosty. Hamlet, waiting on the battlements, says 'The air bites shrewdly; it is very cold', and Horatio answers 'It is a nipping and an eager air' (Hamlet 1.4.1–2). The echo is faint but Rossetti would have known it, and Hamlet too is a play about a hidden truth. 'Nipping' comes back in line 17 ('Nipping and clipping'), and 'biting' picks up the idea of pecking that runs through the poem.

title: Shawl, veil, cloak
short: The winter clothing doubles as a set of concealments: the veil in particular suggests modesty, the nun's habit, or the bride.
body: In the list 'a shawl, / A veil, a cloak, and other wraps', literal protection against cold becomes a figure for reserve. The veil carries strong associations. It belongs to the religious woman (Rossetti's sister Maria later became an Anglican nun), to the bride, and to Victorian ideals of female modesty. The cloak is the traditional sign of concealment. The poem thus makes the speaker's privacy look like common sense, since nobody goes out into the cold uncovered.

anchor: I cannot ope to every one
title: ope to every one who taps
short: 'Ope' is the poetic form of 'open'. The image of someone tapping at the door may echo the biblical knocking at the door (Revelation 3:20; Song of Songs 5:2).
body: 'Ope' was already archaic and poetic by Rossetti's day. In this line the self is a house, and the visitors who 'tap' would let cold draughts 'whistling through my hall'. Readers who know Rossetti's devotional poetry may hear a reversal of Revelation 3:20 ('Behold, I stand at the door, and knock'), which Holman Hunt had famously painted in The Light of the World (1853–54), and of the lover knocking in Song of Solomon 5:2. Here the knocking is resisted, not welcomed. The echo is possible, not certain. Either way the house image makes reticence an act of self-protection.

anchor: I wear my mask for warmth
title: Mask
short: The speaker openly says she wears a mask but presents it as practical shelter, not deceit.
body: This is the poem's most quoted line. It admits disguise and at the same time makes it harmless, since the mask is 'for warmth'. Many critics see in it a statement of Rossetti's poetics of reserve. On this reading the lyric 'I' is a persona, not a confession, and the reader who demands self-revelation is being refused. The line also plays on the convention of the coquette's mask. The reader's protest ('You would not peck?') is answered politely, but the truth is left 'untested still'.

title: Russian snows
short: Russian snows stand for extreme cold. In 1857 the phrase may also have recalled the recent Crimean War winters.
body: 'Russian snows' is a proverbial figure for the harshest cold. It may also have been topical, since the poem was written in 1857, just after the Crimean War (1853–56), whose winters before Sevastopol had been widely reported in Britain. The rhetorical question ('who ever shows / His nose') makes a comic general case of it: no sensible person exposes his face 'To be pecked at by every wind'. The comic diction (nose, pecked) keeps the passage light.

anchor: March with its peck of dust
title: peck of dust
short: This alludes to the old proverb that a peck of March dust is worth a king's ransom (a dry March bodes well for the harvest), and puns on 'pecked' above.
body: A peck is a measure of dry volume, a quarter of a bushel. The proverb 'A peck of March dust is worth a king's ransom' holds that a dry March is good for farming. The speaker distrusts even this lucky sign. The word also puns on the earlier 'peck' (to strike with the beak, ll. 20–21), so the threatening winds and the curious listener are carried into spring. In this stanza each spring month is undercut in turn: March's dust, April's 'brief showers', and May's flowers, which a frost may 'wither'.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'peck, n.1'

title: Summer day
short: Only in a ripe, balanced summer, when it is neither too sunny nor too cloudy, might the secret be spoken, and even then it is only a 'perhaps'.
body: The last stanza imagines ideal conditions: drowsy birds, fruit 'ripening to excess', wind 'neither still nor loud'. The conditions are so finely balanced that they may never come. The phrase 'golden fruit is ripening to excess' carries a hint of sensual danger. It recalls the forbidden fruit of 'Goblin Market' in the same 1862 volume, and the Romantic language of ripeness in Keats's 'To Autumn'. The seasons have run from refusal to a deferred possibility, but the speaker still promises nothing.

title: Or you may guess
short: The poem ends by giving the task back to the reader: the secret may be told, or it may already be guessable.
body: The short last line is a deliberate anticlimax. It may mean that the reader will someday guess the secret unaided, or that the poem has already given it away, or that guessing is all a reader of lyric ever does. Critics who read the poem as a statement about poetics stress this last move. The reader is shut out of the speaker's inner life and is left in the position of interpreter. The poem's rhyme and rhythm, as well as its sense, stay open to the end.
